Insights into the highly selective and efficient adsorption of Pb2+ by fish skin collagen-enabled sodium alginate-based composite gel spheres: adsorption and interference mechanisms

Zuomiao Yang [a](#_bookmark0), Yu Liu [a](#_bookmark0), Enze Wang [a](#_bookmark0), Wei Yin [c](#_bookmark2), Yujiao Wang [a](#_bookmark0), Yicheng Guo [a](#_bookmark0),

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Fish skin collagen Sodium alginate Compound gel spheres

A B S T R A C T

Excessive lead content in wastewater and seaweed products is an urgent scientific problem to be solved. Sodium alginate (SA) is often used as a synthetic gel material to adsorb Pb2+ due to its good biocompatibility and affinity for metal ions. However, simple SA gels suffer from poor mechanical stability and limited adsorption capacity for Pb2+. Therefore, there is a need to develop a stable composite SA gel material with high adsorption capacity for Pb2+. Fish skin collagen (FC), as a by-product, is not highly utilized at present, and its own rich amino and carboxyl groups, is a natural and environmentally friendly food-grade adsorbent alternative material. Sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), a polysaccharide rich in carboxyl groups, is also a good raw material for the preparation of new and safe composite SA gels. Therefore, in this study, a green and non-toxic CMC-FC-SA composite gel sphere was developed to adsorb Pb2+ efficiently by physically mixing SA/CMC/FC in the framework of a one-pot method with Ca2+ cross-linking. The prepared porous composite gel spheres not only had good swelling and thermal stability, but also showed excellent specific adsorption capacity for Pb2+. The results revealed that the adsorption process of CMC-FC-SA on Pb2+ was more consistent with the proposed secondary kinetic model and Langmuir isothermal adsorption model, suggesting that the adsorption process was governed by monolayer chemisorption. The maximum theoretical value of Qm for Pb2+ adsorption was determined to be

586.56 mg/g, and the thermodynamic results indicated that the adsorption of Pb2+ was an unprompted exothermal reaction. However, the adsorption mechanism of the composite spheres is not yet clear. Therefore, the adsorption mechanism of Pb2+ on CMC-FC-SA was revealed to be dominated by ion-exchange reactions and ligand interactions, supplemented by physical adsorption by characterization such as FTIR and XPS. Notably, the CMC-FC-SA spheres displayed good removal efficiency (>88 %, under the Pb2+ residue limit of GB.) for Pb2+ in

the five seaweed concentrates and could maintain the quality of seaweed concentrates. The effect of coexisting

organic matter fractions in seaweed concentrates on adsorption has not been evaluated. Therefore, interference tests revealed that SA, phlorotannins and fucoxanthin antagonized Pb2+ adsorption through hydrogel diffusion blocking, hydrophobic cluster competition for coordination and micelle adsorption, respectively. While mannitol, glutamate and aspartate enhanced the removal rate by solubilization via -OH/-COOH complexation, synergistic mass transfer via bidentate chelation and hydrophilic optimization. The green strategy proposed in this study provides an efficient adsorbent for treating water and regulating heavy metal content in seaweed products.

# Introduction

Brown algae, such as _Laminaria japonica_ and _Undaria pinnatifida_, accumulate heavy metals like lead (Pb) due to their high polysaccharide and alginate content, with Pb concentrations influenced by environ-mental pollution and species-specific metal-binding capacities ([Andrade](#_bookmark29) [et al., 2010](#_bookmark29); [Cheng et al., 2019](#_bookmark43)). Pb toxicity poses severe health risks, including neurotoxicity, developmental delays, and cardiovascular damage ([Collin et al., 2022](#_bookmark45)), prompting the WHO to enforce strict Pb intake guidelines (Organization, 2022). Reducing Pb levels in seaweeds through clean water sources and controlled cultivation is critical to ensuring their safety and health benefits ([Paz et al., 2019](#_bookmark77)). In addition, during the processing of seaweed juice concentrates, the original Pb2+ in seaweeds is easily enriched due to water evaporation and volume reduction, resulting in a significant increase in its concentration. Sea-weeds are strongly adsorbent to heavy metals due to the presence of polysaccharides and alginates, but the concentration process exacer-bates the accumulation of Pb2+, which may threaten food safety. Therefore, lead removal treatment is a key link to ensure the safety of seaweed products.

Various technologies are employed for lead removal, including ion exchanging ([Dong et al., 2019](#_bookmark47)), electrochemical methods ([Liu et al.,](#_bookmark68) [2013](#_bookmark68)), membrane removal ([Bhatluri et al., 2015](#_bookmark33)), chemical coagulation ([Chen et al., 2018](#_bookmark42)), and adsorption ([Ali & Gupta, 2006](#_bookmark28)). Among them, adsorption has numerous advantages such as high efficiency, low cost, versatility and renewability ([Al-Amrani and Onaizi, 2024](#_bookmark27); [Mane et al.,](#_bookmark73) [2024](#_bookmark73)). Adsorption is particularly advantageous because it can be tailored to specific applications, offers high selectivity for metal ions, and can be utilized in both industry and the environment ([Rajendran](#_bookmark79) [et al., 2022](#_bookmark79)). Adsorbent materials are broadly categorized into metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) ([Lin et al., 2023](#_bookmark66); [Naghdi et al., 2023](#_bookmark75)), covalent-organic frameworks (COFs) ([Wang et al., 2023](#_bookmark89); [Wang &](#_bookmark91) [Zhuang, 2019](#_bookmark91)), and bio-based materials ([Boccia et al., 2023](#_bookmark34); [Ren et al.,](#_bookmark81) [2016](#_bookmark81)). Each of these traditional adsorbents has its own advantages and disadvantages. MOFs and COFs offer high surface area, tunable struc-tures, and strong adsorption capacity, but face challenges in terms of cost, scalability, and stability. COFs show excellent chemical stability but are complex to synthesize and have limited functionalization. Bio-based materials, although safe and biocompatible for environmental and food applications, tend to have low adsorption efficiency and limited selectivity in complex environments. In summary, current ad-sorbents generally suffer from high production costs, insufficient selec-tivity under practical conditions, lack of targeted functionalization, and poor reusability. Therefore, for lead removal from seaweed juice con-centrates, it is crucial to develop a green and safe economical, efficient, selective and renewable adsorbent.

Natural and safe polymer biomaterials such as SA ([Zhao et al., 2021](#_bookmark105)),

CMC ([Chen et al., 2019](#_bookmark41)) and proteins ([Liao et al., 2020](#_bookmark65); [Zhang et al.,](#_bookmark102) [2022](#_bookmark102)) are adsorbents applicable in the food field. CMC is a water-soluble derivative of cellulose, modified by introducing carboxymethyl groups (-CH2\-COOH) into the cellulose backbone ([Najihah et al., 2024](#_bookmark76)). CMC’s carboxymethyl groups provide active sites for chelating heavy metals like Pb2+. It is highly water-soluble, making it easy to integrate into composite materials for adsorption. Its low cost, non-toxicity, and eco-friendliness make it a practical choice for heavy metal removal ([Sheraz et al., 2025](#_bookmark82)).

SA is a naturally occurring macromolecular anionic polysaccharide derived from brown algae, consisting of β-D-mannuronic acid (M) and α-L-guluronic acid (G) units ([Ye et al., 2024](#_bookmark99)). SA is abundant in hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, which can form stronger coordination with metal ions such as Pb2+(Huang & Wang, 2018). In addition, it can form hydrogel spheres through cross-linking with calcium ions, providing a stable structure for adsorption. Due to its good biocompatibility and good complexation of heavy metal ions ([Liu et al., 2022](#_bookmark67)), SA has been more extensively employed in Pb2+ removal studies. Li et al. constructed a graphene-containing sodium alginate gel sphere for adsorption of

waste water containing lead ions, and the results demonstrated that their composite gel sphere had good adsorption capacity and regener-ation performance ([Li et al., 2024](#_bookmark62)). Guerrero et al. designed a sodium alginate-chitosan composite composite gel material for the removal of Pb2+ and Cu2+ using an in-situ generation method, and the results demonstrated that their composite gel spheres had good adsorption capacity ([Guerrero et al., 2024](#_bookmark51)). In addition, the enhancement of removal of metal ions and dye pollutants by functionalization of modi-fied sodium alginate composites has also been investigated ([He et al.,](#_bookmark55) [2025](#_bookmark55); [Kim et al., 2025](#_bookmark59)). In summary, SA composites are constantly being optimized and innovated, and currently the adsorption of Pb2+ is mainly synergistically enhanced through the compounding of materials enriched with multiple functional groups and functionalized modifica-tions. However, the introduction of proteins as functional carriers has been less studied in favor of polysaccharides and some organic mate-rials. It is noteworthy that the current research on lead removal is more in the environmental field and less in liquid food research applications. In addition to CMC and SA, FC also possesses the potential to adsorb Pb2+. FC is derived from aquatic processing wastes (e.g., fish skin) and consists mainly of amino acids such as glycine, proline, and hydroxy-proline ([Majeed and Rather, 2024](#_bookmark72); [Rajabimashhadi et al., 2023](#_bookmark78)). The abundant amino and carboxyl groups of FC can effectively bind heavy metal ions such as Pb2+ through chelation and electrostatic interaction. In addition, it is biodegradable, biocompatible, and nontoxic, making it suitable for food and biomedical applications. Currently, the main focus on the utilization of fish skin collagen is on the development of wound healing materials ([Cai et al., 2024](#_bookmark36)), antidiabetic peptides ([Munawaroh](#_bookmark74) [et al., 2023](#_bookmark74)), and carriers for the encapsulated delivery of active in-gredients ([Xiao et al., 2025](#_bookmark93)), however, there are few reports on its development as an environmentally friendly adsorbent. Turning dis-carded fish skins into functional adsorbent materials of high-quality proteins not only reduces the waste of resources, but also has great commercial value. Therefore, FC was introduced as a functional protein

to empower and energize the SA-CMC composite gel.

Overall, most of the current adsorption materials are primarily uti-lized in simple aqueous systems, with limited application in complex food systems such as seaweed concentrates. The adsorption field lacks truly green materials suitable for complex food systems. The safety and efficiency of the material is the primary concern. The fish skin collagen resources rich in various functional groups derived from fish processing by-products can be used as raw materials for developing green and efficient adsorbents. Furthermore, there is a lack of research on the adsorption mechanisms of lead by composite gel materials made from sodium alginate (SA) and fish skin collagen (FC). It is worth noting that there are multiple components in seaweed juice concentrates, and these coexisting organic components can adsorb with some interference. Little has been reported on the mechanism of interference with Pb2+ in complex systems. To address this gap, this study aims to develop a green, safe, and non-toxic all-biomass gel material using SA, carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), and FC through a simple one-pot method. The research focuses on focusing on its adsorption mechanism of Pb2+ in water and seaweed concentrates and the interference mechanism of coexisting organic substances. The novel green-functional protein-polysaccharide composite hydrogel adsorbent developed in this study has great poten-tial to effectively remove heavy metals from seaweed concentrates and aqueous systems, contributing to safer food processing practices and water purification.

# Material and methods

- 1.  _Chemicals_

Sodium alginate (purity ≥99.70 %, molecular weight: 100 kDa, viscosity: 20-100 mPa-s), anhydrous calcium chloride (purity ≥99.50

%), sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (purity ≥99.80 %, molecular weight: 700 kDa, viscosity: 600-1200 mPa-s), fish skin collagen (purity

≥98 %) were procured from Beijing Solaibao Technology Co., Ltd, China. Lead nitrate (purity ≥99.99 %) was purchased from Tianjin Damao, China. All chemical reagents used are analytical grade. Dried _Laminaria japonica_ was purchased from Shanghai Sanyuan Industry Co., Ltd. in China, _Undaria pinnatifida_ was purchased from Dalian Liaohai Aquatic Food Trading Co., Ltd. in China, _Sargassum fusiforme_ was pur-chased from Wenzhou Jiahai Food Co., Ltd. in China, and _Ascophyllum nodosum_ and brown algae residue were all supplied by Qingdao Mingyue Seaweed Group Co.

- 1.  _Synthesis of CMC-FC-SA spheres_

The preparation of CMC-FC-SA composite spheres is demonstrated in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark5). The ingredients – SA (0.5 g), CMC (0.5 g) and FC (0.5 g) – were meticulously weighed and amalgamated with 55 mL of deionized water.

- 1.  _Swellability performance, Zeta potential test and pH stability_

Precisely 25 mg of freeze-dried CMC-FC-SA spheres were taken in 50 mL of de-ionized water at 25 ◦C, and the aqueous solution was brought to dissolution equilibrium at different pH (pH = 2.0–7.0) by dropwise addition of hydrochloric acid solution (0.1 M) or NaOH (0.1 M). The pH value of the solutions was ascertained through the utilization of a pH meter. Following dissolution equilibrium, the spheres were then sub-jected to a careful removal of excess water from their surface by means of filter paper. Subsequently, the weight of the spheres was detected. The balance swellability ratio (ESR) of the CMC-FC-SA spheres was then calculated according to equation [(1)](#_bookmark4) ([Wang et al., 2025](#_bookmark86)):

The co-mixture was stirred on a rotary stirrer for 120 min to form a uniform solution. The resultant complex solution was then gradually introduced into a 4 % CaCl2 solution via a 5 mL syringe, where it was left

- 1.  _Characterization_

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Thermo Kalpha, USA) was employed to analyze the elements and chemical bond states of the spheres. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) instrument (Spectrum Two, Japan) is used to analyze functional group changes in materials. The crystal structure of the materials was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) (10KVA, Japan). The heat resistance properties of the composites were analyzed by thermal gravimetric analyzer (TGA) (TGA500, USA). The emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (JSM-7800F, Japan) was used to view the micro morphology of the prepared materials. The zeta potential of the prepared material was measured with a zeta potentiometer (90PlusZeta, UK). The BET specific surface area and average pore size of the synthetic spheres were char-acterized by Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET, Mike ASAP2420, USA). Moreover, isothermal adsorption modelling tests were conducted at 298 K, 308 K and 318 K respectively. Following the attainment of equilibrium in the adsorption process, the concentration of residual Pb2+ present in the solution was subsequently determined by means of atomic absorption spectrophotometry. - -   1.  _Co-existing ion interference test_

To evaluate the role of coexisting cations on the removal of Pb2+, four cations (K+, Na+, Ca2+ and Mg2+) with different competitive characteristics were dissolved in 50 mL of Pb (II) solution at 50 mg/L at five different concentrations (0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 and 0.25 M). Sub-sequently, CMC-FC-SA spheres were incorporated into the aforemen-tioned mixed samples and subjected to adsorption experiments in a thermostatic water bath oscillator at 298 K and 100 rpm for a duration of 24 h.

To examine the potential for reuse of CMC-FC-SA spheres, 50 mg of CMC-FC-SA spheres were mixed with 50 mg/L Pb2+ solution for adsorption for 24 h. After each adsorption, the composite gel spheres adsorbed with Pb ions were then desorbed through the process of im-mersion in 15 mL of an eluent solution of 0.1 M HNO3 for a period of 6 h. The regeneration experiment was repeated in five cycles.

- -   1.  _Extraction of seaweed juice concentrates and their Pb2_+ _removal_

Firstly, 10 g of normal dried seaweed or brown algal scum were selected and soaked in 1 L of deionized water. Then, the seaweed and deionized water were pulped at a mass-to-volume ratio of 1 g:100 mL to obtain the seaweed slurry. Next, the seaweed slurry was heated at 50 ◦C for 12 h; then filtered and concentrated to 100 mL of seaweed juice concentrate by heating at 100 ◦C, and finally filtered again to obtain seaweed juice concentrate. Based on the previous most suitable adsorption conditions, a certain amount of CMC-FC-SA spheres were

then placed respectively into various seaweed concentrates containing 50 mL for oscillation adsorption.

- -   1.  _Interference test for Pb2_+ _adsorption by major components of seaweed juice concentrate_

Due to the complex composition of seaweed concentrates, multiple food components can interfere with Pb2+ removal. Therefore, in view of the comprehensive assessment of the effects of components on adsorp-tion, the main representative components of brown algal concentrate were selected as modeling interfering factors, including SA, mannitol, glutamic acid (Glu), aspartic anhydride (Asp), brown algal polyphenol (Phl) and fucoxanthin (FX). Sequentially, these certain masses of inter-fering factors and CMC-SA-FC spheres were put into 50 mg/L Pb2+ so-lution for coexistence adsorption, and the control group was the treatment group without interfering factors or water as solvent. Finally, the spheres were collected after adsorption was completed and then dried and used for FTIR analysis to reveal their interference mechanism.

- -   1.  _Effect of adsorption of Pb2_+ _on changes in the quality of seaweed juice concentrates_

Before and after removal, the color, pH and soluble solids content of the four seaweed concentrates were tested separately. The colorimeter (3nh, TS7000, Shenzhen, China) was calibrated and then the color of the seaweed concentrates was measured at the same location at room tem-perature. The pH meter was calibrated and the pH of different seaweed concentrates was determined separately at room temperature. The hand-held refractometer was first zeroed with deionized water, dried the in-spection mirror, put in 1–2 drops of seaweed juice concentrate, and gently covered the plywood. Finally, held flat against the light, adjusted the eyepiece until the light and dark demarcation was clear, and recorded the readings.

- 1.  _Data statistics_

The results of the experiment were expressed as mean ± standard and analyzed by Duncan’s one-way ANOVA.

# Result and discussion

- 1.  _Characterization_
        1. _SEM-EDS analysis_

As illustrated in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark11)a, the CMC-FC-SA composite spheres appeared as grayish-white spheres after being freeze-dried. The internal micro-structure of CMC-FC-SA before and after adsorption of Pb2+ was

examined using SEM, as demonstrated in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark11)b–c. Before adsorption, the material showed an irregular gel 3D meshed macroporous nature. with a substantial total surface area, and this large honeycomb structure with macroporous pores and close interconnections was beneficial to rapidly facilitated diffusion. and binding of Pb2+ to the active sites during the adsorption process. Similarly, the interior of the bovine skin collagen-sodium alginate-tannin extract composite aerogel spheres synthesized by Zhao et al. also showed an irregular macroporous structure observed by SEM ([Zhao et al., 2025](#_bookmark106)). When the CMC-FC-SA spheres adsorbed lead ions, the folds inside the composite spheres increased significantly, and the whole material showed a honeycomb porous morphology with randomly distributed pores of different sizes. Compared with before adsorption, the diameter of these pores became smaller, and the reticular structure was more closely connected, which may be caused by the removal of a significant quantity of Pb2+ in the material and the formation of complexes caused by the pore filling effect.

In order to determine the elemental composition of SA-CMC-FC before and after removal, EDS energy spectroscopy was performed. According to [Fig. 2](#_bookmark11), it was seen that before and after the adsorption, the elements nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), carbon (C), and calcium (Ca) were evenly dispersed throughout the material. And after the adsorption, the presence of the element Pb was able to be detected, which was mainly concentrated on the surface of the material, which confirmed that SA-CMC-FC could effectively adsorb Pb2+. In addition, the relative con-tent of Ca2+ decreased after removal, suggesting that ion exchange took place during the adsorption process.

- -   1.  _XRD analysis_

As shown in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark12)a, SA was a linear polysaccharide (composed of G/ M blocks) with a predominantly amorphous structure, characterized by broad peaks at 2θ = 13◦ (corresponding to G-block stacking) and 2θ = 22◦ (attributed to disordered M-blocks) ([He et al., 2022](#_bookmark54)). CMC also exhibited a broad "steamed bread-like" peak centered at 2θ = 20◦. Similarly, FC displayed a broad peak near 2θ ≈ 22◦, indicative of its amorphous regions. CMC and SA were crosslinked via hydrogen bonding and Ca2+ coordination, which enhanced the network stability. The resulting CMC-SA composite showed further broadening of XRD peaks, reflecting a further reduction in crystallinity. FC interacted with SA/CMC through its amino (-NH2) and carboxyl (-COOH) groups, while its hydrophobic domains participated in self-assembly. The SA-FC composite primarily exhibited broad peaks, but two sharp peaks emerged at 2θ = 31◦ and 45◦, likely originating from short-range or-dered regions formed by Ca2+ crosslinking and hydrophobic aggregation of FC. SA and CMC formed a network skeleton through Ca2+

**Fig. 3.** XRD spectras of SA, CMC, FC, SA-CMC, SA-FC and CMC-SA-FC spheres (a); FTIR spectras of SA, CMC, FC, SA-CMC, SA-FC and CMC-SA-FC spheres (b) and the curves of TGA of SA, CMC, SA-CMC, SA-FC and CMC-SA-FC spheres (c).

crosslinking, while FC was embedded into the network voids via hy-drophobic interactions or hydrogen bonding, ultimately forming core-shell structured CMC-FC-SA hydrogel spheres. Notably, the incor-poration of CMC did not disrupt the ordered regions of SA-FC but instead enhanced network stability through hydrogen bonding, preserving the short-range order. This was evidenced by the XRD pattern of CMC-FC-SA, which retained the broad peaks and the characteristic sharp peaks of SA-FC at 2θ = 31◦ and 45◦. These sharp peaks were attributed to Ca2+\-crosslinked short-range ordered regions and collagen hydrophobic aggregation. In summary, the XRD patterns of CMC-FC-SA could be observed that the characteristic peaks of SA and CMC were significantly weakened or disappeared, and the two characteristic sharp peaks of SA-FC were retained, which results strongly proved that the three of them were formed into a new type of composite material through chemical cross-linking reaction. In a similar manner, Chen et al. discovered that the XRD spectrum of the synthesized magnetic SA-based hydrogel bead adsorbent further demonstrated the elimination of the SA characteristic peak, whilst concurrently exhibiting the retention of a single distinctive peak ([Chen et al., 2025](#_bookmark40)).

- -   1.  _FTIR analysis_

The changes in the FTIR spectrum of the CMC-FC-SA spheres were illustrated in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark12)b. As observed in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark12)b–O-H/N-H stretching vi-brations occurred near 3500 cm—1 ([De la Cruz et al., 2022](#_bookmark46); [Wang et al.,](#_bookmark86) [2025](#_bookmark86)). The hydroxyl groups (-OH) of SA (3427 cm—1) merged with the amino groups (-NH2) of FC (3400 cm—1) into a broad peak, suggesting the presence of a hydrogen-bonding network among these groups. The hydroxyl groups of CMC further participated in this hydrogen-bonding network, enhancing the three-dimensional stability of the hydrogel material. Additionally, carboxylate group vibrations were observed near 1600 cm—1 and 1450 cm—1 ([Yang et al., 2022](#_bookmark98)). The asymmetric stretching vibration peak of -COO\- in SA (1657 cm—1) merged with the peak of CMC (1608 cm—1), confirming the formation of an "egg-box" structure (SA-COO-⋅⋅⋅Ca2+⋅⋅⋅OOC-CMC) through Ca2+ crosslinking. The symmetric-COO-stretching vibrations were moved towards lower wave numbers (redshift), reflecting the restricted vibrational modes of the carboxylate group due to Ca2+ coordination. Notably, C-H stretching vibrations near 2800 cm—1 were also observed ([Li et al., 2023](#_bookmark60)). This sharp peak was attributed to the ordered aggregation of hydrophobic side chains in FC (e.g., proline, leucine), which correlated with the sharp XRD peaks at 31◦ and 45◦ in CMC-FC-SA. In summary, the successful synthesis of CMC-FC-SA was verified by comparing the FTIR spectrums of CMC, SA, FC, and their composites. The spectral changes demon-strated synergistic interactions, including hydrogen bonding, Ca2+ crosslinking, and hydrophobic assembly, which collectively contributed to the structural integrity and functionality of the hydrogel spheres.

- -   1.  _Thermogravimetric analysis_

The thermogravimetric results were shown in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark12)c. The thermal degradation processes of the five materials were basically similar during

the change from 30 ◦C to 600 ◦C. The CMC-FC-SA spheres basically retained the thermal degradation properties of SA, CMC and FC, which indicated that the CMC-FC-SA spheres were successfully synthesized. When CMC-FC-SA was specifically analyzed, the mass loss was roughly divided into three levels. The first level was 30◦C–230 ◦C, where the weight loss was slower (16.11 %) owing to the vaporization of water from CMC-FC-SA spheres ([Archana et al., 2013](#_bookmark30)). The second stage was 230◦C–355 ◦C, where the samples underwent a rapid decomposition process (mass loss of 25.94 %), which was attributed to the high-temperature-induced thermal degradation of the biomass material, with breakage and degradation of polysaccharide chains (e.g., glycosidic bond breakage of SA and CMC), breakage of peptide bonds of fish skin collagen, and decomposition of amino acid residues occurring mainly ([Liu et al., 2016](#_bookmark69)). As the temperature elevated to 600 ◦C, the trend of the thermal weight loss line was the smoothest (9.55 % mass loss), and the mass loss of the samples was mainly caused by the carbonisation of re-sidual organic matter. Finally, the residual mass percentage of CMC-FC-SA was 51.60 %. In addition, according to the comparison of the five curves in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark12)c, the residual amount after thermal decompo-sition of CMC-FC-SA was significantly higher than the other four ma-terials, which can prove that the number of oxygen-containing functional groups acting as cross-linking increases in the ternary com-posite system of CMC-FC-SA, and higher cross-linking density would drive up the thermo-degradation temperature, thus improving the thermal stability of the composite spheres ([Cheikh et al., 2020](#_bookmark39)). Similar studies were reported for ternary SA-based composite gel spheres exhibiting excellent thermal stability due to highly crosslinked and enriched matrix by TGA analysis (Liu et al., 2023).

- -   1.  _XPS analysis_

XPS was employed to analyze the chemical element species and chemical bond binding energy changes in the CMC-FC-SA spheres. N1s, O1s, C1s and Ca2p peaks could be observed in the full XPS spectrum of the CMC-FC-SA spheres as depicted in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)c. The presence of Ca2p characteristic peaks confirmed the success of cross-linking. As demon-strated in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)e, the C1s fine spectra exhibited peaks at 284.80 eV,

286.30 eV, and 288.40 eV, corresponding to C-C, C-N, and C=O bonds,

respectively ([Wang et al., 2025](#_bookmark86)). In addition, as displayed in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)f, the N1s fine spectra presented two peaks at 400.01 and 402.00 eV, corre-sponding to C=N and C-N, respectively ([Li et al., 2022](#_bookmark61)). The presence of the N1s peaks indicated that the FC was successfully involved in the material synthesis and that its nitrogen-containing functional group might have formed a coordination bond with Ca2+. In addition, the fine spectra of O1s in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)f displayed three characteristic peaks at 531.70,

532.50 and 533.20 eV, which were attributed to C=O, -OH and -C-O-C,

respectively ([Cai et al., 2023](#_bookmark35)). These characteristic peaks indicated that the oxygen-containing functional groups in SA, CMC and FC were crosslinked with Ca2+. Combined with the previous EDS, XRD and FTIR results, the XPS results also provided further evidence for the successful synthesis of CMC-FC-SA spheres.

- -   1.  _Swelling and zeta potential analysis_

Swelling property is the capacity of hydrogel materials to absorb and expand in water, which directly affects their adsorption properties ([Lv](#_bookmark71) [et al., 2019](#_bookmark71)). The swelling property of the material greatly improves the adsorption capacity and adsorption rate by enlarging pores, exposing sites and optimizing mass transfer. As illustrated in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark13)c, the swell-ability of CMC-FC-SA was strongest at pH = 6 and gradually weakened

after pH > 6. When pH = 2–6, the deprotonation of carboxylic acid

(-COO-) of the material leads to the enhancement of electrostatic repulsion and the solubility gradually increases. At pH = 6, the Ca2+crosslinked ‘egg carton’ structure remains stable, balancing elec-trostatic repulsion with crosslink strength, and swelling is maximised. In circumstances where the pH value exceeds 6, electrostatic repulsion may prove to be excessively potent. This, in turn, has the potential to result in partial rupture of the crosslinked network, a decline in the material’s mechanical strength, and an augmentation in the degree of swelling. Therefore, at pH = 6, the high solubility of the material ensures the complete exposition of the adsorbing sites, and the electrostatic attrac-tion and mass transfer efficiency synergistically enhance the adsorption capacity. The good swelling property facilitates the carboxylate to ex-change ions with Pb2+ more easily (replacing Ca2+), while the swollen network makes it easier for the amino group (-NH2) and hydrophobic side chains of the FC to form a polydentate complex with Pb2+ (e.g., Pb-OOCR-NH-FC). In addition, at pH = 6, the hydrophobic side chains of FC (e.g., leucine, phenylalanine) remain moderately aggregated, providing hydrophobic adsorption sites, while solubility ensures the accessibility of hydrophilic sites (-COO\-). Furthermore, Tang et al. (2022) discovered that SA hydrogels exhibited enhanced swelling properties in a weakly acidic environment (pH ≥ 5), thereby facilitating the removal of cations ([Tang et al., 2020](#_bookmark83)). In conclusion, the removal performance of CMC-FC-SA on Pb2+ was synergistically determined by pH-modulated surface charge, swelling properties and lead ion morphology.

The Isoelectric Point (IEP) is defined as the pH level where a mate-rial’s surface charge becomes neutral. As shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark13)b, the com-posite gel sphere formed by CMC-FC-SA reached the Isoelectric Point at pH = 2.30, when the carboxylic acid group (-COOH) of SA/CMC was protonated and the amino group (-NH+) of FC was positively charged,

3

and the positive and negative charges canceled out each other. With increasing pH (pH > 2.30), the carboxylic acid group of SA/CMC dis-sociates to -COO\- and the amino group of FC is deprotonated and the

carboxylic acid group dissociates to -COO\-, resulting in a sharp rise in face negative charge density and an increase in the absolute value of the potential, at which time the carboxylic acid group and Pb2+ (positive charge) generated a strong electrostatic attraction, which was favorable for adsorption. At pH < 2.30, CMC-FC-SA was protonated and the sur-

face was positively charged ([Han et al., 2022](#_bookmark53)), at which time the

adsorption of Pb2+relied on a non-electrostatic mechanism (e.g.,

coordination or ion-exchange), which was less efficient. In contrast, the surface negative charge is enhanced at high pH (e.g., pH = 5–6), which significantly enhances the Pb2+ adsorption capacity through electro-static attraction and chelation ([Xiang et al., 2024](#_bookmark92)). In addition, too high pH (e.g., >7) and the generation of Ca (OH)2 might disrupt the gel structure, which was unfavorable for adsorption. Therefore, determi-

nation of the isoelectric point of CMC-FC-SA helped to optimize the pH range in removal of Pb2+.

- -   1.  _Analysis of BET specific surface area and porosity of CMC-FC-SA spheres_

The porosity of the CMC-FC-SA spheres was investigated by nitrogen physisorption at 77.30 K. As illustrated in Table S1, the analysis based on the BET theory and the Barret-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) method showed that the specific surface area and the average pore size of the CMC-FC-SA spheres were 1.61 m2/g and 4.69 nm, respectively. As shown in Fig. S1a, the N2 adsorption-desorption isotherm of CMC-SA-FC composite gel spheres displayed a typical IV-type isotherm with an obvious H3 hys-teresis loop, indicating the presence of mesopores in the material ([Gao](#_bookmark49) [et al., 2023](#_bookmark49)). In addition, the pore size distribution was mainly concentrated in the range of 0–40 nm (Fig. S1b), which was mesoporous in nature, and this mesoporous structure was favorable for the Pb2+ adsorption performance.

- -   1.  _Analysis of pH stability of CMC-FC-SA spheres_

The pH stability of the CMC-SA-FC composite gel spheres is shown in Fig. S2, where the structural changes were observed in the pH = 2–10 range at 12 and 24 h, respectively. From [Fig. 2](#_bookmark11)a and Fig. S2, it could be seen that the gel spheres were able to absorb water and undergo swelling phenomenon and maintain good structural integrity, no matter in acidic, neutral or alkaline environments. The pH stability results were basically consistent with the swelling results, i.e., the gel swelling ability was best at pH = 6, which was favorable for the diffusion of water and Pb2+ into the CMC-SA-FC composite gel spheres, thus improving the adsorption capacity. Similarly, Wang et al. reported different swelling phenomena of sodium alginate-chitosan composite hydrogels at different pH ([Wang](#_bookmark86) [et al., 2025](#_bookmark86)). Notably, in this study, no cracking or precipitation of the synthesized materials was observed, suggesting that the synthesized materials have good stability at pH, which is favorable for the applica-tion of lead removal from seaweed juice concentrates.

- -   1.  _Superiority analysis of CMC-FC-SA composite spheres for Pb2_+ _removal_

The superiority of CMC-FC-SA composite spheres for Pb2+ removal is shown in Fig. S3, where one-component gel spheres (SA, for example) and two-component gel spheres (SA-CMC and SA-FC, for example) were far inferior to the CMC-FC-SA composite spheres for the removal of Pb2+ at the same dosage and adsorption conditions. The CMC-FC-SA

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 4.** Variation of adsorption capacity of CMC-SA-FC spheres for Pb2+ at different pH (a); curves of zeta potential map variation of CMC-SA-FC spheres at different pH (b) and swelling property of CMC-SA-FC spheres at different pH (c).

composite spheres had the highest adsorption rate, which indicated that SA, CMC and FC enhanced the removal of Pb2+ through synergistic ac-tion. This was closely related to the abundant functional groups and stable structure in the CMC-FC-SA composite spheres. Therefore, the CMC-FC-SA composite spheres were selected as the best adsorbent for subsequent adsorption experiments.

- 1.  _Adsorption characteristics_
        1. _Dosage of CMC-FC-SA spheres_

The effect of CMC-FC-SA dosage (20–100 mg) on Pb2+ adsorption is presented in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark14)a. [Fig. 5](#_bookmark14)a displayed higher adsorption rates with greater adsorbent amounts. The higher removal rate resulted from greater adsorbent dosage and more reactive sites (e.g., carboxyl -COO\-, amino -NH2) provided by the materials, which allowed the adsorption of more Pb2+ and increased the overall removal rate ([Ren et al., 2013](#_bookmark80)). In addition, at high doses, the density of adsorbent particles in solution increases, shortening the average distance of Pb2+ diffusion to the active site and accelerating the removal speed. When the quantity of CMC-FC-SA spheres reached 80 mg, 95 % of Pb2+ (initial 50 mg/L) had been removed from the solution, and the remaining Pb2+ concentration was extremely low (≈2.5 mg/L), close to the detection limit or adsorption equilibrium concentration. However, at high doses, the adsorbent particles may aggregate due to electrostatic or hydrophobic effects, which reduces the effective specific surface area, resulting in some of the internal sites not being accessible to Pb2+ (El-Shafey, Obada, El-Shamy, & Mohamed, 2024). In addition, at high doses, the remaining quantity of Pb2+ was extremely low, adsorption was saturated, and excess adsorbent did not continue to enhance the adsorption capacity ([Zhao et al., 2021](#_bookmark105)). Therefore, the selection of adsorbent dosage needs to be considered targeted and economical. Based on the considerations of efficient removal of Pb2+ from seaweed juice concentrate and green economy, we chose 80 mg as the additive amount for further tests.

- -   1.  _pH_

The pH of water affects how heavy metal ions behave by altering their adsorbent surface charge ([Wang et al., 2015](#_bookmark84)). It is imperative to ascertain the optimal adsorption pH for the effective execution of the removal process. The effect of different pH values on the removal of

Pb2+ was examined as demonstrated in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark13)a. Within the pH range of 3–7, the removal capacity exhibited a maximum at pH = 6, subsequently decreasing. The underlying reason for this phenomenon was that, at low pH (e.g., pH = 3), the carboxylate (-COO\-) of CMC-FC-SA protonated, i. e., converts to -COOH, which lost its negative charge and weakens the electrostatic attraction with Pb2+. Similarly, the amino group (-NH2) is protonated to form -NH+, which is electrostatically repelled from Pb2+. Therefore, low pH caused a decrease in reaction sites, resulting in a decrease in removal capacity. When the medium solution was at medium-high pH (e.g., pH = 6), the carboxylate deprotonation (-COO\-was negatively charged, which enhanced the electrostatic attraction with Pb2+) and the amino acid deprotonation (-NH2 stayed neutral or weakly negatively charged, which reduces the repulsion effect) of CMC-FC-SA, and therefore, the material had the maximum surface negative charge density and the adsorption capacity reaches its peak. However, at pH ≥ 7, Pb2+ was either hydrolyzed or precipitates as Pb (OH)2, reducing the free Pb2+ concentration ([Wang et al., 2025](#_bookmark86)); furthermore, excessive deprotonation might weaken the crosslinked network and reduce the mechanical strength of the material, which ul-timately led to a decrease in the amount of adsorption ([Wang et al.,](#_bookmark88) [2013](#_bookmark88)). In addition, the morphology of Pb2+ also affected its adsorption effect. When pH = 6, Pb2+ was predominantly in the free state (Pb2+), and the adsorption sites were sufficiently exposed to be adsorbed effi-ciently by the material, thus reaching the maximum adsorption value. It was worth noting that the material stability was optimal at pH = 6, where the crosslinked network of CMC-FC-SA was complete and the hydrophobic/hydrophilic sites are fully exposed, resulting in the opti-mum removal potential. More importantly, at a pH of 6, the -COO\- and Ca2+ cross-linking sites of CMC-FC-SA were efficiently replaced by Pb2+, and the -NH2 of FC formed a stable complex with Pb2+ under the weakly acidic condition, and the hydrophobicity of FC increased which pro-vided additional adsorption sites. Consequently, CMC-FC-SA exhibited the most pronounced removal capacity for Pb2+ at a pH of 6.

- -   1.  _Temperature_

3

The temperature exerts a primary influence on the removal effect, affecting both the surface charge distribution of the material and the ion diffusion in the aqueous solution. Therefore, adsorption experiments were conducted at different temperatures to screen for the optimal

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 5.** Effect of different doses of CMC-SA-FC spheres (a), contact time (b), and different temperatures (c) on the adsorption of Pb2+ by CMC-SA-FC spheres; thermodynamic curves obtained from fitting (d).

temperature, and the results were shown in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark14)c. As demonstrated in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark14)c, an increase in adsorption temperature was observed to occur in a gradual manner, the adsorption rate of Pb2+ by the CMC-FC-SA spheres decreased from 97.70 % to 91. 32 %, which may be due to the following reasons: (1) Adsorption is an exothermic process (ΔH < 0), and

increasing the temperature will disrupt the adsorption equilibrium (Le

Chatelier’s principle), which consequently lead to an enhancement of desorption and a reduction in the removal rate. (2) Higher temperatures may lead to relaxation or degradation (e.g., hydrogen bond breaking) of the hydrogel crosslinking network, reducing the stability of the active site (e.g., carboxylate). (3) Although the high temperature accelerated the diffusion of lead ions, it also prompted the adsorbed Pb2+ to be more easily desorbed and diminished the interaction forces between the ad-sorbents. Overall, CMC-FC-SA may react exothermically for Pb2+ adsorption and inhibit adsorption at high temperature ([Yang et al.,](#_bookmark96) [2023](#_bookmark96)). At 25 ◦C, the CMC-FC-SA gel spheres reached a favorable state for Pb2+ adsorption in terms of thermodynamics, structural stability, intermolecular interactions, diffusion and desorption equilibrium, and surface properties to achieve the optimal adsorption effect. Therefore, all subsequent experiments were conducted at a constant temperature of 25 ◦C.

- -   1.  _Adsorption time_

As exhibited in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark14)b, the removal process of Pb2+ by CMC-FC-SA was found to be comprised of three distinct periods. The initial phase was the fast reaction phase, during which the amount adsorbed increased rapidly within the 90 min. This phenomenon could be attributed to the existence of a substantial number of functional sites (e. g., carboxylate -COO\-, amino -NH2) on the surface of CMC-FC-SA, which rapidly bound Pb2+ by electrostatic attraction, ion exchange and coor-dination ([Li et al., 2021](#_bookmark63)). Meanwhile, the high initial concentration of Pb2+ facilitated rapid adsorption. In this phase, the diffusion of Pb2+ to the material surface was a rate-controlled step with a superior removal rate. In the middle stage (from 90 to 210 min), internal diffusion dom-inates, when the surface sites were gradually saturated and Pb2+ needed to penetrate the pores of the material to diffuse internally at a slower rate. The adsorption process reached the third stage around 210–360 min, when the adsorption reached dynamic equilibrium (360 min), the active sites were close to saturation, the removal rate exhibited a ten-dency to be 100 %, and the adsorption reached equivalence with an adsorption capacity of about 117 mg/g.

- -   1.  _Co-existing ionic strength_

The coexistence of multiple ions in wastewater and seaweed prod-ucts often occurs, especially metal cations may compete with Pb2+ for adsorption, thus inhibiting the adsorption ability of the adsorbent. To assess the competitive effect of coexisting ions, four common heavy metal ions, Na+, K+, Ca2+, and Mg2+, were selected as competitive ions for Pb2+, and the results were illustrated in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark16). The removal of Pb2+ was found to be inhibited by metal ions, and the higher the ion con-centration, the stronger the inhibition effect. The impact of Mg2+ and K+ on the removal of Pb2+ was found to be minimal, with the adsorption level consistently maintained at approximately 50 mg/g. On the con-trary, Ca2+ had the greatest competitive effect on Pb2+, and its adsorption performance was significantly weaker than that of the other two ions. This phenomenon was closely related to the electronegativity ([Guo et al., 2017](#_bookmark52)), hydration energy, functional group affinity and structural properties of the ions. The strongest inhibitory effect of Ca2+ was attributed to the formation of carboxylate “egg carton” model in CMC-FC-SA by cross-linking, and the development of “egg carton” structure of free Ca2+ in solution, which occupied a large number of adsorption sites. In addition, free Ca2+ in solution can directly replace adsorbed Pb2+ by ion exchange, and Ca2+ has a stronger affinity for carboxylic acid radicals than Pb2+, especially during material synthesis, where Ca2+ has already formed a crosslinked network. In addition, high concentrations of Ca2+ may disrupt the original cross-linking network,

leading to reduced solubility of the material and reduced accessibility of the active site. The high concentration of Na+ (monovalent ions) attenuated the electrostatic force between the negative charges on the face of the material and Pb2+through the electrostatic shielding effect ([Jiang et al., 2020](#_bookmark58)). A large amount of Na + occupied some of the low affinity sites and reduced the removal opportunities of Pb2+. Further-more, the presence of Na+ had a secondary effect of reducing the exposure of reaction sites. This was achieved by means of alterations to the ionic strength of the water environment, the compression of the double electric layer on the surface of the adsorbent, and the inhibition of the swelling of the hydrogel network ([Ajouyed et al., 2010](#_bookmark26)). On the contrary, Mg2+ had a higher hydration energy (1922 kJ/mol) than Ca2+ (1577 kJ/mol) and Pb2+ (1480 kJ/mol) and it was difficult to remove the hydration layer, and the coordination efficiency with carboxylates was low. K+, a monovalent cation with low charge thickness, had a much weaker electrostatic force with carboxylates than Pb2+ and its competitiveness was limited. In summary, ion exchange (Ca2+) and electrostatic shielding (Na+) were the main reasons for inhibition, and Mg2+ and K+ had limited influence due to their poor physicochemical properties.

- -   1.  _Adsorption kinetics_

To gain a comprehensive understanding of the removal behaviour of CMC-FC-SA spheres on Pb2+, the quasi-first-order kinetic (QFO) model and quasi-second-order kinetic (QSO) model were fitted based on the adsorption time of 0–360 min and its corresponding adsorption amount data, respectively, and the fitting results were presented in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark15)a. As illustrated in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark15)a and corroborated by the data presented in [Table 1](#_bookmark17), it was determined that the adsorption had attained dynamic equilibrium at the 330-min mark. The R2 of the QSO model was 0.983, which was higher than that of the QFO model (0.932). Moreover, the calculated equilibrium adsorption value derived from the fitting of the QSO model was 118.360 mg/g, which was more consistent with the actual experi-mental value (115.50 mg/g). In conclusion, the adsorption process of Pb2+ by CMC-FC-SA spheres exhibited greater consistency with the QSO model, which was predominantly characterised by chemisorption ([Zheng et al., 2021](#_bookmark108)).

- -   1.  _Adsorption thermodynamics_

The thermodynamic curve of Pb2+ adsorption on CMC-FC-SA com-posite gel spheres was demonstrated in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark14)d, and the related ther-modynamic parameters were presented in [Table 2](#_bookmark18). By fitting the thermodynamic model curve, it can be concluded that lnKc increases with increasing 1/T (positive slope), and the positive slope meant that

ΔH < 0 (an exothermic process), which agreed with the experimental

results ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark14)c), and exothermic drove the ion exchange. The ΔG at different temperatures were —1835.36, —1864.19, and —1881.80 (KJ/ mol), respectively. ΔG was negative, suggesting that the Pb2+ removal

by the CMC-FC-SA spheres was an unprompted reaction ([Lu et al.,](#_bookmark70) [2025](#_bookmark70)). ΔS (<0) had a physical significance in the sense that the change of Pb2+ from a free state to a stationary state and the ordering of solvent

molecules (e.g., bound water (e.g., release of bound water) led to a decrease in the entropy of the system, thus weakening the adsorption drive. The immobilization process resulted in a decrease in system en-

tropy (ΔS < 0), owing to the creation of coordination bonds between

Pb2+ and carboxyl and amino groups in the material. Therefore, the

dominant mechanism for Pb2+ removal on CMC-FC-SA composite spheres was spontaneous exotherm-driven ion exchange and coordina-tion, and the decrease in entropy and the change in the material struc-ture together limited the high-temperature adsorption performance.

composite spheres for Pb2+ adsorption exhibited a marked enhancement with increasing concentration, with the optimal adsorption outcomes being attained at 298 K. The Langmuir model demonstrated superior fit (R2 = 0.9948) compared to the Freundlich model, clearly showing it was better suited for characterizing Pb2+ adsorption onto CMC-FC-SA com-posite gel spheres. This strong correlation suggested the adsorption

Reusability denotes an adsorbent’s capacity to retain adsorption ef-ficiency and structural integrity through repeated adsorption-desorption cycles ([Chiew et al., 2016](#_bookmark44)). Through regeneration, the material can be reused many times, reducing the material cost and environmental burden in practical applications. As demonstrated in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark20)a, after five repeated uses, the Pb2+ removal by CMC-FC-SA gel spheres decreased significantly (95 %–60 %). The main reason for the deterioration of regeneration might involve irreversible damage to the material structure with the loss of functional groups ([Wang, Liu, et al., 2024](#_bookmark87)). The Ca2+ crosslinked three-dimensional network might undergo solvation rupture

or crosslinking site breakage during repeated acid solution desorption, resulting in a reduction in particular contact area and mechanical strength. Meanwhile, strong acidic desorption conditions could cause protonation or chemical degradation of key adsorption groups, such as

\-COOH of SA and -NH2 of FC, weakening their ligand chelating ability. To verify whether the desorption of 0.1 M HNO3 resulted in the struc-tural disruption of the CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres, the structural changes of the CMC-SA-FC composite gel spheres after regeneration

were recorded by SEM and the results were shown in Fig. S4. As observed in Fig. S4, the pore walls inside the gel spheres became thinner and the pores became larger as the number of regenerations increased, which visually proved that desorption with repeated acid (0.1 M HNO3) caused a certain degree of disruption of the gel network structure. In addition, with repeated regeneration, the structure of the material changes and the adsorption sites decrease, and the SEM results were consistent with the regenerative results.In addition, incomplete

desorption of residual Pb2+ possibly occupied the active site, while partial denaturation (the hydrophobic microenvironment may be dis-rupted, reducing the availability of hydrophobic adsorption sites) or dissolution of FC further reduced the adsorption capacity of CMC-FC-SA spheres ([Zhang et al., 2024](#_bookmark103)). These synergistic effects led to a decline in the regeneration performance of CMC-FC-SA spheres with an increase in the frequency of cycles. Therefore, the regeneration stability of the adsorbent can be improved by strengthening the cross-linking structure, optimizing the desorption conditions and functional group protection.

- 1.  _The adsorption mechanism of Pb (II)_

To investigate the removal mechanism of Pb2+ on CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres, the aim of the current study was to systemati-cally and comprehensively analyze the changes in the morphology, crystalline shape, reactive groups and chemical bonding of the adsor-bent before and after the adsorption of Pb2+ by a combination of char-acterization tools.

By comparing the SEM changes before and after adsorption (as dis-played in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark11)b–c), the pores become smaller and the gel network structure becomes denser after adsorption, and this experimental result can be a preliminary proof that the surface of CMC-FC-SA has a different structure due to the removal of a significant quantity of Pb2+. This change could be related to physical adsorption such as pore filling and surface physical interception. As depicted in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark11)d–e, the presence of Pb could be detected in the EDS spectra of CMC-FC-SA after adsorption and a significant decrease in the absorption peak signal of Ca could be observed, which further verified that the material could effectively adsorb Pb2+ and that there was an ion-exchange reaction during the removal process. In conclusion, the SEM-EDS results demonstrated that the removal mechanism of Pb2+ on CMC-FC-SA spheres included phys-ical adsorption and ion exchange reaction. Furthermore, as demon-strated in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark13)a–b, zeta potential and pH experiments indicated a robust electrostatic interaction for the removal of Pb2+ by CMC-FC-SA at

pH > pI.

The XRD plots of CMC-FC-SA spheres before and after adsorption were shown in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)a. Prior to the adsorption process, the CMC-FC-SA showed two very distinct sharp peaks near 2θ = 31◦ and 45◦. Howev-er, after adsorption of Pb2+, the two sharp peaks in CMC-FC-SA completely disappeared. This was due to the competitive coordination of Pb2+ and the conformational transition of FC disrupting the Ca2+\-crosslinked gel network, which led to the disappearance of the sharp peaks and the amorphization of the material. The results of XRD proved that the adsorption mechanism of Pb2+ by CMC-FC-SA spheres could be a synergistic effect of ion exchange, multidentate coordination, and structural reorganization.

The FTIR spectra of the CMC-FC-SA compound hydrogel spheres after Pb2+ adsorption were shown in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)b. After adsorption, peak broadening and redshift were observed near 3500 cm—1 (O-H/N-H vi-brations, a shift from 3500 to 3450 cm—1) ([Yu et al., 2017](#_bookmark101)). This was attributed to the coordination of Pb2+ with O-H/N-H groups, forming Pb-O/N bonds, which disrupted the original hydrogen-bonding network ([Zheng et al., 2025](#_bookmark107)). The reduction of free hydroxyl and amino groups, along with hydrogen-bond reorganization, resulted in peak broadening. Near 1600 cm—1 (-COO\- asymmetric stretching vibration), a redshift occurred, specifically from 1631 to 1603 cm—1 ([Yang et al., 2022](#_bookmark98)). This was caused by Pb2+ replacing Ca2+ via ion exchange, forming stronger coordination bonds with carboxylate groups ([Yadav et al., 2021](#_bookmark95)). The increased bond length and reduced vibrational frequency confirmed the ion exchange reaction during adsorption. Similarly, near 1450 cm—1 (-COO\- symmetric stretching vibration), a redshift from 1431 to 1417 cm—1 was observed. This resulted from Pb2+ forming multi-dentate co-ordination (e.g., chelation or bridging) with carboxylate groups, altering their symmetric vibrational modes ([Fan et al., 2022](#_bookmark48)). This redshift change also reflected the coordination of -CO-NH- with Pb2+. Addi-tionally, before adsorption, the CMC-FC-SA composite exhibited a

pronounced peak at 2800 cm—1, which was associated with the ordered hydrophobic aggregation of FC’s side chains (e.g., phenylalanine aro-matic rings, leucine residues). After Pb2+ adsorption, the intensity of this peak significantly decreased. This suggested that Pb2+ penetrated FC’s hydrophobic core, disrupting the ordered stacking of side chains and collapsing the hydrophobic microenvironment. The destruction of hy-drophobic interactions increased material porosity, exposing hidden adsorption sites. In summary, the removal of Pb2+ by CMC-FC-SA resulted from the synergistic effects of ion exchange, multi-dentate co-ordination, and disruption of hydrophobic interactions. These mecha-nisms collectively enhanced Pb2+ binding capacity and structural reorganization of the composite.

To conduct a more in-depth investigation into the mechanism of Pb2+ adsorption by CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres, we analyzed the spectral changes before and after CMC-FC-SA adsorption by XPS. As shown in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)c–d, the Pb 4f signal was detected after adsorption of Pb2+ by CMC-FC-SA with binding energies of 143.80 eV (Pb 4f5/2) and

139.08 eV (Pb 4f7/2). Pb 4f7/2 corresponded to the Pb-O bond (carbox-ylate or hydroxyl ligand), whereas Pb 4f5/2 was the Pb-N bond (amine ligand) ([Zhang et al., 2023](#_bookmark104)). This result could demonstrate that Pb2+ formed coordination bonds with carboxylate (-COO\-), hydroxyl (-OH), and amino (-NH2), thus indicating that the lead has been successfully adsorbed onto the material. In addition, by comparing before and after adsorption, we also found that the intensity of the absorption peak of Ca decreased significantly, indicating that Pb2+ replaced Ca2+ by ion ex-change ([Hu et al., 2018](#_bookmark56)). Further analyzing the C1s peak change, as shown in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)e, the C-C peak (284.80 eV) was not shifted after adsorption, suggesting that the carbon skeleton of the material was stable and did not undergo chemical damage. However, the binding energy of the C-N peak (286.30 eV→ 286.50 eV) increased slightly, which indicated that the -NH2 was engaged in the coordination and the electron cloud abundance of N decreased (the lone pair of electrons was attracted by Pb2+). Whereas, the decrease in binding energy of the C=O peak (288.40 → 288.10 eV) indicated that the carboxylate (-COO\-) was coordinated with Pb2+, and the electronegativity of the oxygen atom was increased (the electron-absorbing effect of Pb2+ leads to the reversed polarisation) ([Azam et al., 2024](#_bookmark31)).The variation of the N1s peaks was shown in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)f, with the C=N peak (400.00 eV) did not change after adsorption, demonstrating that the conjugated NH2 or pyridine ring was not implicated in the reaction. The decrease in binding energy of the C-N peak (402 → 397.40 eV) indicated that the amino group (-NH2) formed a Pb-N coordination bond with Pb2+ and the electron cloud abundance of the N decreased. The change of the C-N peaks in the N 1s suggested that the hydrophobic side chains (e.g., phenylalanine) might be involved in the coordination, which disrupted the original hydrophobic stacking. The disappearance of the sharp peaks in the XRD corroborated the dissolution of hydrophobic microenvironment. increased porosity, promoting Pb2+ diffusion. Similarly, the O1s peak changes as illustrated in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark21)g, where the decrease in bonding energy of C=O (531.70 → 531.20 eV) indicated that the carboxylate oxygen was coordinated with Pb2+ and the electron density was redistributed ([Li](#_bookmark63) [et al., 2021](#_bookmark63)). Similarly, the binding energies of -OH (532.50 → 531.30 eV) and C-O-C (533.20 → 533.10 eV) were both significantly decreased, this result that also suggested that the hydroxyl and ether-bonded oxy-gens were slightly involved in the coordination or were affected by the reorganization of the hydrogen binding network. In conclusion, the removal of Pb2+ by CMC-FC-SA was a result of the synergistic effect of ion exchange, multidentate coordination and structural reorganization.

In summary, as demonstrated in [Fig. 10](#_bookmark22), the adsorption mechanism

of CMC-FC-SA spheres on Pb2+ was dominated by ion exchange reaction and coordination, and some physical adsorption effects, such as pore-filling effect, surface deposition, electrostatic effect and hydrophobici-ty, were also present.

- 1.  _Comparative analysis of the ability of SA-based materials for Pb2_+ _removal_

As illustrated in [Table 4](#_bookmark23), a comparison has been made of the removal capacity of various SA-based adsorbents for Pb2+. By comparison, the CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres had the strongest removal ability, and the Qm of Pb2+ adsorption reached 584.56 mg/g. Due to the abundant functional group synergism among the three natural polymers of SA, CMC, FC, the synergistic effect of multiple functional groups greatly increased the adsorption sites and binding force for lead ions. For example, SA and CMC could provide a considerable quantity of -COOH and -OH, and FC provided abundant amino and carboxyl groups to have ion exchange reaction and coordination with Pb2+. FTIR and XPS results demonstrated the synthesis of CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres and the mechanism of efficient adsorption of Pb2+. In addition, the SEM results demonstrated that the CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres had a stable loose and porous 3D gel network structure, and this highly porous structure not only allowed for the diffusion and transport of Pb2+ inside the material, whilst simultaneously increasing the material’s particular contact area and providing augmented removal sites, thus improving the adsorption efficiency. Therefore, the removal ability of the CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres was superior to that of the magnetic materials,

**Table 4**

Parameters of isothermal adsorption model for Pb2+ adsorption by CMC-SA-FC.

polymer composites, carbon materials and grafted nanocomposites in [Table 4](#_bookmark23). It is important to note that the CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres were not only straightforward to prepare (the one-pot prepa-ration process is simple to operate, reducing preparation time and cost, and facilitating large-scale production), but also exhibited favorable safety and environmental protection characteristics. The materials used are all natural, food-grade, biodegradable substances that will not cause generate additional pollution during use. In conclusion, the safe and environmentally friendly CMC-FC-SA composite gel spheres with excellent adsorption capacity will have great application prospects in food safety control, water purification and soil remediation.

- 1.  _Selective adsorption test_

To verify the high selectivity of CMC-FC-SA for Pb2+, several metal ions were selected for comparison. As presented in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark20)b, all CMC-FC-SA exhibited highly selective adsorption of Pb2+ (adsorption rate close to 100 %), fair adsorption of Cu2+, and almost no adsorption of Cd2+.The highly selective nature of the CMC-FC-SA spheres for Pb2+ was explained by the high coordination ability of the chemical groups of the spheres (-NH2 and -COOH) with Pb2+, coupled with low hydration en-ergy of the Pb2+, easily binds to the adsorbent. On the contrary, Cd2+ was difficult to be adsorbed due to its high hydration energy or lack of suitable coordination groups. Cu2+, on the other hand, was subjected to a distorted coordination configuration due to the Jahn-Teller effect, which resulted in a significantly weaker binding ability to carboxylic acid groups than Pb2+, so the adsorption effect was average. Therefore, the synthesized CMC-FC-SA spheres exhibited high selectivity for the adsorption of Pb2+.

- 1.  _Analysis of CMC-FC-SA spheres for the removal of Pb2_+ _from seaweed juice concentrates_

In order to evaluate whether the CMC-FC-SA spheres can be applied to seaweed juice concentrates, five different seaweed concentrates were prepared for adsorption validation. The removal rates of Pb2+ from the five seaweed concentrates by CMC-FC-SA spheres were shown in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark20)c. The experimental data showed that the CMC-FC-SA spheres exhibited efficient Pb2+ adsorption capacity (88 %–98 %) in all five seaweed concentrates, and the adsorption rates were ranked as follows:

_Sargassum fusiformes_ (98 %) > _Undaria pinnatifida_ (97 %) > _Ascophyllum nodosum_ (95 %) > _Saccharina japonica_ (91 %) > brown algae scum (88

%). According to Table S2, the Chinese standard for lead in common algae products (1.0 mg/kg) is significantly stricter than the WHO/FAO and EU standards (3.0 mg/kg). All the concentrated juices met the GB 2762-2017 lead limit standard (≤1.0 mg/kg) after adsorption, indi-cating that CMC-FC-SA has the potential for practical application in complex seaweed matrices. It was hypothesised that the variations in the removal rates of different seaweed concentrates might be attributable to the complexity of the matrix composition and the morphology of the lead. high efficiency of the adsorption of Pb2+ from seaweed juice concen-

trates by the CMC-FC-SA spheres (88 %–98 %) originated from the carboxyl-amino group synergistic chelation, porous mass transfer

structure and anti-interference ability. The carboxyl group (-COO\-) in the adsorbent dominated ion exchange (Pb2+\-Ca2+ exchange) and electrostatic attraction, and -NH2 and -OH of FC formed a stable chelate with Pb2+. In addition, the hydrophobic microenvironment of FC could reduce the competitive adsorption of polysaccharides or organic acids and enhance the selectivity. Meanwhile, the three-dimensional network gel structure endowed the material with high contact area and abundant pores, which promoted the diffusion and trapping of Pb2+. Notably, the CMC-FC-SA spheres were more resistant to co-existing ions (Na+, K+) and organics (polysaccharides, organic acids), thus favoring the enhancement of Pb2+ adsorption. In conclusion, CMC-FC-SA spheres have excellent adsorption capacity and can be applied to both simple (aqueous solution) and complex systems (seaweed concentrates) for metal cation removal.

- 1.  _Analysis of the effect of the main components of seaweed concentrate on the removal of Pb2_+

In view of investigating the interfering effects of the main compo-nents of seaweed juice concentrate on Pb2+, SA, mannitol, Glu, Asp, Phl and FX were selected as the coexisting organisms. As shown in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark20)d, the results indicated that mannitol, Glu and Asp could synergistically enhance the adsorption rate, while SA, Phl and FX acted as inhibitors of adsorption compared with the control. As a polyol, mannitol, with its abundant hydroxyl group (-OH), could form soluble complexes with Pb2+, enhance the solubility and migration ability of Pb2+ in the aqueous phase, reduce its precipitation or agglomeration, and promote its diffusion to the top of the spheres. In addition, both Glu and Asp contain carboxyl (-COOH) and amino (-NH2) groups, which could form stable complexes with Pb2+ through bidentate coordination, and at the same time direct Pb2+ to the surface of the adsorbent through

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 11.** FTIR spectra of coexisting organics: SA (a), Mannitol (b), Glu (c), Asp (d), Phl (e) and FX (f).

electrostatic attraction. However, SA cross-linked with Ca2+ to form a dense three-dimensional gel, which significantly increases the solution viscosity, restricts the free diffusion of Pb2+, and reduced its contact frequency with the adsorption sites. Meanwhile, the gel network phys-ically coverd the top of CMC-FC-SA spheres (e.g., CMC, FC), masking the functional groups such as carboxyl and amino groups, which directly reduced the number of effective reactive sites. Similarly, Phl aggregated into micrometer-sized particles in the aqueous phase due to lipid solu-bility, blocking the pore channels of CMC-FC-SA spheres; it also occu-pied the surface of the material by physical buildup, preventing Pb2+ from approaching the active sites. Finally, the lipid solubility induced the formation of micelles or precipitates of FX, which were adsorbed on the top of the gel spheres to form a hydrophobic interfacial layer, hin-dering the cross-interfacial migration of polar Pb2+. In addition, the conjugated structure of FX loosely bound Pb2+ through the π-π inter-action, which dispersed and immobilized Pb2+ inside the micelles, detaching it from the main adsorption pathway and decreasing the targeting adsorption efficiency. Overall, mannitol, Glu and Asp enhanced the Pb2+ adsorption efficiency through complexation solubi-lization, mass transfer promotion and hydrophilic microenvironment optimization; whereas SA, Phl and FX inhibited the adsorption process through physical blocking, spatial site-blocking and non-targeted adsorption, separately.

- 1.  _Interference mechanism of Pb2_+ _removal by coexisting organic matter in seaweed juice concentrates_

In view of further exploring the interference mechanism of the main components of the seaweed juice concentrate with Pb2+, the changes of FTIR spectra of the coexisting organics were analyzed. As indicated in [Fig. 11](#_bookmark24)a, when SA coexisted with Pb2+, the CMC-FC-SA spheres were red-shifted at the vicinity of 3450 cm—1. This reflected the -COOH-Pb2+ ligand-dominated interaction, which led to the binding of Pb2+ inside the SA network through hydroxyl deprotonation, gel structure rigidity enhancement, and competitive adsorption, while inhibiting the adsorption capacity of the composite gel spheres. Further, as illustrated in [Fig. 11](#_bookmark24)b, Mannitol showed a blue shift near 3450 cm—1 (O-H stretch vibration) and 1620 cm—1 (C-O stretching vibration or H-O-H bending vibration of the water molecule) in the FTIR spectra when it was coex-isted with Pb2+, indicating that Mannitol specifically interacts with Pb2+. This suggested its mechanism of promoting adsorption through solubilization by hydroxyl complexation, optimization of mass transfer channels and dynamic synergism. Similarly, as demonstrated in [Fig. 11](#_bookmark24)c, Glu showed a blue shift around 1600 cm—1 (-COOH asymmetric tele-scoping vibration) and 1400 cm—1 (-COOH symmetric telescoping vi-bration) when coexisting with Pb2+, suggesting that Glu’s -COOH interacted specifically with Pb2+ by liganding ([Wang et al., 2018](#_bookmark85)). This phenomenon mirrored the dominant facilitation of -COOH-Pb2+ chela-tion, which significantly enhanced the migration efficiency and acces-sibility of the reaction site for Pb2+ through bidentate coordination solubilization, amino-synergistic electrostatic modulation and hydro-philic channel optimization.

Similar to the Glu results, as illustrated in [Fig. 11](#_bookmark24)d, the coexistence of (Asp) with Pb2+ resulted in a redshift in the FTIR spectra at 3400 cm—1 (O-H/N-H stretch vibration), and the redshift in the FTIR spectra at 1620 cm—1 (-COOH asymmetric stretching vibration) and 1400 cm—1 (-COOH symmetric stretch vibration)) and 1400 cm—1 (-COOH sym-metric stretching vibration) appeared blue-shifted, suggesting that Asp forms a dynamic complex system with Pb2+ through multiple coordi-nation ([Chauhan & Bordes, 2025](#_bookmark38)). This result suggested that Asp formed a dynamic complexation system through the synergistic effect of -COOH strong chelation (blue shift) and -OH/NH2 weak coordination (red shift) to achieve solubilization, directional migration and efficient adsorption of Pb2+. The FTIR spectra of CMC-SA-FC composite gel spheres for the coexistence of Phl with Pb2+, as illustrated in [Fig. 11](#_bookmark24)e, were observed at 3450 cm—1 (O-H/N-H stretching vibration) and 1620 cm—1

(-COOH/-NH2 vibration) near the red shift, while Phl itself exhibited a blue shift at 3450 cm—1 (phenolic hydroxyl O-H vibration) and 1620 cm—1 (phenolic ring C=C vibration). This double spectral shift revealed a synergistic mechanism by which Phl interfered with Pb2+ adsorption through competitive coordination with hydrophobic clustering. Simi-larly, as illustrated in [Fig. 11](#_bookmark24)f, the FTIR spectra of CMC-SA-FC spheres were red-shifted around 3450 cm—1 (O-H/N-H stretching vibration) and 1620 cm-1 (-COOH/-NH2) when FX was coexisting with Pb2+, whereas the spectrum of FX itself was red-shifted around 3450 cm—1 (-OH or hydration vibration) redshifted and 1620 cm—1 (conjugated double bond or lipid soluble group vibration) blue-shifted. This dual spectral shift revealed a synergistic mechanism of FX inhibition of Pb2+ adsorption through interfacial adsorption competition with hydrophobic cluster blocking. This result was in agreement with the interference adsorption results ([Fig. 8](#_bookmark20)d).

Overall, SA, Phl and FX, as interfering components, inhibited Pb2+ adsorption through hydrogel-blocked diffusion (SA), hydrophobic clustering with competing coordination (Phl) and micellar interfacial adsorption (FX), respectively; whereas mannitol, glutamic acid (Glu) and aspartic acid (Asp) significantly improved the removal efficiency through solubilization via the complexation of the -OH/-COOH root (mannitol), bidentate chelating-mass transfer synergism (Glu/Asp) and hydrophilic microenvironment optimization significantly enhanced the removal efficiency.

- 1.  _Analysis of changes in the quality of seaweed juice concentrates_

[Table 5](#_bookmark25) summarizes the changes in quality of CMC-FC-SA spheres before and after adsorption of Pb2+ on four brown algal concentrates. As can be seen from the table, there was no significant effect on the color, pH and soluble solids content of _Saccharina japonica_, _Undaria pinnatifida_, _Sargassum fusiformes_ and _Ascophyllum nodosum_ concentrates after adsorption. This demonstrated that the CMC-FC-SA spheres mainly exerted a strong affinity for Pb2+ in the seaweed juice concentrates, and had less effect on other organic components. On the contrary, the metal-framed aerogel material reported by Li et al. not only adsorbed heavy metal ions in pear juice, but also absorbed some components such as organic acids and sugars ([Li et al., 2025](#_bookmark64)). This might be related to the selective adsorption strength of the adsorbent. These experimental findings also provided strong evidence that the CMC-FC-SA spheres exhibited a high selective adsorption of Pb2+ and could effectively maintain the quality of seaweed concentrates.

# Conclusions

In this study, a composite hydrogel sphere based on CMC, FC and SA (CMC-FC-SA) was successfully developed and prepared by one-step physical blending with Ca2+ cross-linking method, which possesses green and safe, high adsorption performance (maximum adsorption up to 584.56 mg/g) and good thermal and pH stability and selectivity, and it is suitable for the water and many kinds of seaweed concentrates for

Highly efficient removal of Pb2+ (removal rate >88 %, up to 97 %). The current maximum removal rate can reduce the Pb2+ concentration in

algal concentrates to below the Pb2+ residue limit for seaweed products in the Chinese national standard. The study indicated that the adsorp-tion behavior was in accordance with the Langmuir isothermal model and the QSO model, and the mechanism was dominated by ion exchange and ligand interaction, and the excellent performance was still main-tained in the complex organic matrix. Regarding component interfer-ence, SA, Phl and FX inhibited Pb2+ adsorption through diffusion blocking, hydrophobic cluster competition for coordination and micellar interfacial adsorption, whereas mannitol, Glu and Asp significantly enhanced the removal efficiency through complexation solubilization, bi-dentate chelating synergy and microenvironmental optimization. Overall, scientifically, the mechanism of multi-component synergistic enhancement of adsorption capacity was revealed, expanding the
